# sysutils_limits (Resource)

Manages one `pam_limits` entry, `<domain> <type> <item> <value>`, in a drop-in file in `/etc/security/limits.d`, below the provider's `root_dir` if that is set. Several `sysutils_limits` resources can share a file; comments and all other lines in it are kept, and the file's mode and ownership are preserved. Changes are written atomically. On destroy only the entry is removed, and the file too if the provider created it and nothing else is left in it. The limits apply to sessions that start after the change. Requires root privileges, unless used with `root_dir` on a tree you can write.

`pam_limits` sets resource limits, such as the number of open files or processes, when a session starts: at login, with `su` or `sudo`, and for cron jobs. It covers the same ground as editing `limits.conf` by hand, or Ansible's `community.general.pam_limits` module. Services started by systemd don't go through PAM; set `LimitNOFILE=` and similar in their unit, for example with [`sysutils_ini_value`](./ini_value.md) in a drop-in.

## Example Usage

### Limits for a user, a group, everyone and a UID range

```terraform
# Let the postgres user open up to 65536 files. Both entries go to
# /etc/security/limits.d/90-terraform-user-postgres.conf, the default file
# for the domain.
resource "sysutils_limits" "postgres_nofile_soft" {
  domain = "postgres"
  type   = "soft"
  item   = "nofile"
  value  = "65536"
}

resource "sysutils_limits" "postgres_nofile_hard" {
  domain = "postgres"
  type   = "hard"
  item   = "nofile"
  value  = "65536"
}

# Let members of the "audio" group lock memory without limit, for both the
# soft and the hard limit ("-").
resource "sysutils_limits" "audio_memlock" {
  domain = "@audio"
  type   = "-"
  item   = "memlock"
  value  = "unlimited"
}

# No core dumps for anyone, in /etc/security/limits.d/90-terraform-default.conf.
resource "sysutils_limits" "no_core_dumps" {
  domain = "*"
  type   = "hard"
  item   = "core"
  value  = "0"
}

# Regular users, by UID range, get at most 4096 processes.
resource "sysutils_limits" "users_nproc" {
  domain = "1000:"
  type   = "hard"
  item   = "nproc"
  value  = "4096"
}
```

### Several entries in one file

```terraform
# All limits of one application in a file of its own, one resource per
# entry. Other lines in the file, such as comments added by hand, are kept.
locals {
  app_limits = {
    "soft-nofile" = { type = "soft", item = "nofile", value = "16384" }
    "hard-nofile" = { type = "hard", item = "nofile", value = "65536" }
    "both-nproc"  = { type = "-", item = "nproc", value = "8192" }
  }
}

resource "sysutils_limits" "app" {
  for_each = local.app_limits

  domain = "app"
  type   = each.value.type
  item   = each.value.item
  value  = each.value.value
  file   = "80-app.conf"
}
```

## Schema

### Required

- `domain` (String) Who the limit applies to: a user name such as `"postgres"`, a group as `"@developers"`, `"*"` for everyone, a UID range as `"1000:1999"`, `"1000:"` (1000 and above) or `":1000"` (exactly 1000), a GID range as `"@1000:1999"`, or, for the `maxlogins` and `maxsyslogins` items only, `"%"`, `"%group"` or `"%:<gid>"`. Names may only contain letters, digits and `_.-`, and a final `$`; a numeric name is refused, as `pam_limits` would compare it with names, not IDs. Changing this forces a new resource.
- `item` (String) The limit to set: `as`, `core`, `cpu`, `data`, `fsize`, `locks`, `maxlogins`, `maxsyslogins`, `memlock`, `msgqueue`, `nice`, `nofile`, `nonewprivs`, `nproc`, `priority`, `rss`, `rtprio`, `sigpending`, `stack`. See `limits.conf(5)` for what each one means and its unit. Changing this forces a new resource.
- `type` (String) `"soft"` for the limit processes start with, `"hard"` for the ceiling up to which unprivileged processes may raise it, or `"-"` for both. Changing this forces a new resource.
- `value` (String) The value, as a string: a non-negative integer, or `"unlimited"`, `"infinity"` or `"-1"` for no limit. `nice` and `priority` take a nice value from `-20` to `19` and have no unlimited; `nonewprivs` takes `0` or `1`. The spellings of unlimited, and numbers with leading zeros, are compared as the same value, so they are not drift.

### Optional

- `file` (String) Name of the drop-in file in `/etc/security/limits.d`, such as `"90-postgres.conf"`. It is created with mode `0644` if needed, starting with a comment line that marks it as created by the provider. Must be a plain file name ending in `.conf`, of letters, digits and `_.-+@`, not starting with `.` or `-`: `pam_limits` ignores other files, and a name can't refer to a file outside the directory. Defaults to a name derived from `domain`: `"90-terraform-user-postgres.conf"` for `"postgres"`, `"90-terraform-group-developers.conf"` for `"@developers"`, `"90-terraform-default.conf"` for `"*"` and `"90-terraform-uid-1000-1999.conf"` for `"1000:1999"`, so entries for one domain share a file. Changing this forces a new resource.

### Read-Only

- `id` (String) `<path>:<domain>:<type>:<item>`, the import ID.
- `path` (String) Absolute path of the drop-in file, `/etc/security/limits.d/<file>`, inside the provider's `root_dir` if set.

## Entries

The resource manages one line of the form `<domain> <type> <item> <value>`, as described in `limits.conf(5)`. The line is identified by `domain`, `type` and `item`, so changing any of them replaces the resource, and a changed `value` rewrites the line in place.

| `domain` | Applies to |
|----------|------------|
| `"postgres"` | The user `postgres`. |
| `"@developers"` | Members of the group `developers`, including those for whom it is a supplementary group. |
| `"*"` | Everyone; the default for users that no more specific entry matches. |
| `"1000:1999"`, `"1000:"`, `":1000"` | Users with a UID from 1000 to 1999, of 1000 and above, or exactly 1000. |
| `"@1000:1999"`, `"@1000:"`, `"@:1000"` | Users whose primary group has a GID in the range; `"@:1000"` also matches the other members of the group with GID 1000. |
| `"%"`, `"%admins"`, `"%:1000"` | With `maxsyslogins`, all logins on the system; with `maxlogins`, all logins of the members of a group, by name or GID. |

If several entries match, `pam_limits` prefers an entry for the user over one for a group, and one for a group over `*`. Between equally specific entries, the one read last wins: `limits.conf` is read first, then the files in `limits.d` in alphabetical order. That is why the default file names start with `90-`.

`type = "soft"` is the limit a session starts with, `type = "hard"` the ceiling to which an unprivileged process may raise its soft limit, and `type = "-"` sets both. Keep a soft limit at or below the hard limit that applies to the same session.

## Validation

Everything is checked when Terraform plans, before any file is touched:

- `domain` must have one of the forms above. User and group names may only contain letters, digits and `_.-`, and a final `$`; a numeric name is refused, because `pam_limits` would compare it with names, not IDs. In a range, the minimum must not be greater than the maximum. The `%` domains are only accepted with `maxlogins` and `maxsyslogins`, the only items `pam_limits` applies them to.
- `type` must be `soft`, `hard` or `-`, and `item` one of the items listed above.
- `value` must be a non-negative integer or `unlimited`, `infinity` or `-1`, which all mean no limit. `nice` and `priority` take a nice value from `-20` to `19`, and `nonewprivs` takes `0` or `1`.
- `file` must be a plain file name ending in `.conf`, without `/` and not starting with `.`, so it can't refer to a file outside `/etc/security/limits.d`, and `pam_limits` reads it.

## The Drop-in File

The file is edited like `sysctl.d` files by [`sysutils_sysctl`](./sysctl.md): the new content is written to a temporary file next to it and renamed into place, keeping the file's mode, owner, group, ACLs and SELinux label. The edit is abandoned if the file was changed by someone else in the meantime. Edits of one file are serialized, including those of other resources and of other Terraform runs on the host, so several resources can share a file.

- Comments, blank lines and all other entries stay exactly as they are. As in `pam_limits`, a `#` starts a comment anywhere in a line, and commented-out entries never match. Entries are matched as `pam_limits` reads them: the type, item and value are compared ignoring case (`postgres SOFT NOFILE 4096` is the same entry as `postgres soft nofile 4096`), the domain is compared exactly, and fields are separated by ASCII white space only, so a line with a Unicode space between its fields is not an entry.
- An existing entry with a different value is replaced in place; new entries are appended at the end.
- If the file has the entry several times, `pam_limits` uses the last one. Refresh warns about the extra entries, and the next apply that changes the resource removes them.
- A missing file is created with mode `0644`, owned by the user running Terraform, along with `/etc/security/limits.d` if needed. It starts with a comment line that marks it as created by the provider.
- Destroy removes only the entry. The file is deleted when nothing but that first comment line and blank lines is left in it. A file the provider did not create, or one to which lines were added by hand, is kept, even if it is empty.
- A symlink at the file is refused rather than written through. Directories on the way, such as `/etc/security`, may be symlinks; below `root_dir`, they are resolved inside it.

With the provider's `root_dir` set, the file is `<root_dir>/etc/security/limits.d/<file>`, and `path` shows the path inside the tree.

## Drift Detection

On refresh the provider reads the file:

- If the entry's value differs, the plan shows the value on disk, and the next apply writes the configured one again. The spellings of unlimited, and numbers with leading zeros, are the same value to `pam_limits`, so `infinity` in the file and `"unlimited"` in the configuration are not drift.
- If the entry or the file was removed, the resource is removed from the state, and the next apply creates the entry again.

## Behavior

- **Create** refuses an entry that is already in the file, because destroying the resource would remove it. Import it instead. The file's other lines don't matter.
- **Update** rewrites the entry with the new value.
- **Destroy** removes the entry, and the file as described above.

Limits apply to sessions that start after the change. Running processes, including your own shell, keep theirs.

## Import

An existing entry can be imported with `<path>:<domain>:<type>:<item>`, where `path` is the drop-in file. The path ends at the first colon, and type and item are the last two fields, so the domain may contain colons:

```shell
# By <path>:<domain>:<type>:<item>, where path is the drop-in file in
# /etc/security/limits.d.
terraform import sysutils_limits.postgres_nofile_soft /etc/security/limits.d/90-terraform-user-postgres.conf:postgres:soft:nofile

# Domains may contain colons, as UID and GID ranges do.
terraform import sysutils_limits.users_nproc /etc/security/limits.d/90-terraform-uid-1000.conf:1000::hard:nproc
```

`file` is the file name from the path; set it in the configuration unless it is the default for the domain, or the resource is replaced. `value` is read from the file.

## Caveats

- Only files in `/etc/security/limits.d` are managed, not `/etc/security/limits.conf`. Entries in `limits.conf` are read first, so an equally specific entry in a drop-in overrides them.
- The resource does not check whether the user or group exists; `pam_limits` ignores entries that match nobody.
- Whether `pam_limits` runs depends on the PAM configuration: most distributions enable it for logins, `su`, `sudo` and cron, but Debian leaves it commented out in `/etc/pam.d/su`. Alpine only has `/etc/security` with `linux-pam` installed.
- Linux caps `nofile` at `fs.nr_open`, 1048576 by default, and recent versions of `pam_limits` use that cap for `unlimited`. Raise it with [`sysutils_sysctl`](./sysctl.md) for higher values.
